subjective.question: Discuss the importance of water in food.
subjective.answer: Water is the major constituent of most fresh foods (milk contains about 87% and meat about 70-75% water) and it performs many essential functions. (1) It acts as a universal solvent and medium in which nutrients, enzymes and chemical reactions of food take place. (2) It gives food its texture, juiciness and mouthfeel; loss of water makes food dry and tough. (3) It is essential for the growth of microorganisms, so the amount of available water largely decides how quickly a food will spoil. (4) It takes part in chemical changes such as hydrolysis of carbohydrates, proteins and fats. (5) It helps in heat transfer during cooking and processing. (6) In the human body it transports nutrients and removes waste products. Because of these roles, controlling the water of a food (by drying, freezing, or adding salt/sugar) is the basis of most food-preservation methods.

subjective.question: What is water activity (aw)? How does it affect the shelf life of a food?
subjective.answer: Water activity is the ratio of the vapour pressure of water in a food to the vapour pressure of pure water at the same temperature. It measures the water that is actually available (free) for microbial growth and chemical reactions, not the total moisture. Pure water has aw 1.0. Most bacteria need aw above about 0.91, yeasts about 0.88 and moulds about 0.80; below aw 0.60 no microorganism can grow. Therefore the lower the water activity, the longer the shelf life: dried fruits, biscuits and milk powder (low aw) keep for months, whereas milk and meat (aw about 0.98-0.99) spoil within days. Preservation methods such as drying, salting and sugar addition work by lowering aw.

subjective.question: Differentiate between bound water and free water in foods.
subjective.answer: Free water is the water that is loosely held in a food, can be removed easily by pressing or drying, acts as a solvent, freezes readily and is fully available for microbial growth and chemical reactions. Bound water is the fraction of water that is tightly attached to food constituents such as proteins and carbohydrates through hydrogen bonding; it does not freeze at normal freezing temperatures, cannot act as a solvent, and is not available to microorganisms. A food spoils according to its free water (water activity), not its total water, which is why two foods with equal moisture content can have very different keeping quality.

subjective.question: Write a note on raw milk.
subjective.answer: Raw milk is the milk obtained from a healthy animal (cow, buffalo, goat) which has not been pasteurized or given any heat treatment. It is a complete and highly nutritious food containing about 87% water, 3.5-4% fat, about 3.3% protein (mainly casein), about 4.8% lactose and 0.7% minerals and vitamins. Because it is rich in nutrients and has a near-neutral pH (6.6-6.8), raw milk is an excellent medium for microorganisms. It may carry dangerous pathogens picked up from the udder, the animal, the milker or utensils, e.g. Salmonella, Listeria, Campylobacter, pathogenic E. coli, Brucella and the tuberculosis bacillus, which can cause serious food-borne diseases. Raw milk therefore spoils quickly, must be kept refrigerated, and should be boiled or pasteurized before consumption to make it safe.

subjective.question: Give the average chemical composition of cow's milk and name the function of each major component.
subjective.answer: Average cow's milk contains: water about 87%, fat 3.5-4%, protein about 3.3%, lactose about 4.8% and ash (minerals) about 0.7%. Water acts as the medium in which all other components are dissolved, suspended or emulsified. Fat, present as small globules, is the richest source of energy and carries the fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E and K. Proteins (about 80% casein and 20% whey proteins) build and repair body tissues and give milk its curd-forming property used in cheese making. Lactose, the milk sugar, provides energy and helps in the absorption of calcium. Minerals, especially calcium and phosphorus, are needed for bones and teeth, and the vitamins support growth and health.

subjective.question: Why is the consumption of raw milk considered a health risk? Name the important pathogens associated with it.
subjective.answer: Raw milk has received no heat treatment, so any microorganism that enters it during production survives and multiplies rapidly because milk is a rich, near-neutral food. Contamination can come from an infected udder (mastitis), the animal's skin and dung, contaminated water, utensils and the hands of the milker. Important pathogens reported from raw milk include Salmonella typhimurium (food poisoning), Listeria monocytogenes (listeriosis, dangerous in pregnancy), Campylobacter jejuni (diarrhoea), Escherichia coli O157:H7 (haemorrhagic colitis), Brucella species (undulant fever), Mycobacterium bovis (tuberculosis) and Coxiella burnetii (Q fever). Boiling or pasteurization destroys these organisms, which is why health authorities advise against drinking raw milk, especially for children, pregnant women and old people.

subjective.question: What is colostrum? How does it differ from normal milk?
subjective.answer: Colostrum is the thick, yellowish milk secreted by the mammary gland during the first few days (about 3-5 days) after calving. It differs from normal milk in several ways: it contains much more protein, especially immunoglobulins (antibodies) which protect the newborn calf against infections; it is richer in vitamin A, minerals and total solids; it contains less lactose; and it coagulates on heating because of its high albumin and globulin content. Colostrum is not used for normal market milk or cheese making, but it is essential food for the newborn animal.

subjective.question: What is mastitis? Discuss its effects on the quality of milk.
subjective.answer: Mastitis is the inflammation of the udder (mammary gland), usually caused by bacterial infection, commonly Staphylococcus, Streptococcus and E. coli. It may be clinical (visible swelling, clots and flakes in milk) or sub-clinical (detected only by tests such as the California Mastitis Test and raised somatic cell count). Mastitic milk has increased somatic cells and chloride, decreased lactose, casein and fat, a salty taste and a higher pH. Such milk has poor keeping quality, gives lower cheese yield, is unfit for consumption, and antibiotic residues from treatment can enter the milk. Prevention includes clean milking, teat dipping, dry-cow therapy and regular testing of animals.

subjective.question: Name the common adulterants of milk and the simple tests used to detect added water.
subjective.answer: Common adulterants of milk include added water, starch, urea, detergents, neutralizers, skim-milk powder and removal of fat (skimming). Added water is the most common fraud. It is detected by: (1) the lactometer test - added water lowers the specific gravity of milk below the normal 1.028-1.034; (2) the freezing-point test - pure milk freezes at about -0.52 to -0.55°C, and added water raises the freezing point towards 0°C, so this is the most reliable test; (3) a fall in total solids and solids-not-fat (SNF) also indicates watering. Starch is detected by the iodine test (blue colour) and urea by specific chemical test kits.

subjective.question: What is pasteurization? Describe its main methods and importance.
subjective.answer: Pasteurization is the controlled heat treatment of milk (below boiling) which kills the pathogenic microorganisms and most spoilage organisms without greatly changing the taste and nutritive value. The main methods are: (1) LTLT or holder method - 63°C for 30 minutes, used for small batches; (2) HTST or flash method - 72°C for 15 seconds, the standard commercial method; (3) UHT treatment - 135-150°C for 1-4 seconds, giving milk that keeps for months without refrigeration until opened. Pasteurization makes milk safe from diseases like tuberculosis, brucellosis and Q fever (Coxiella burnetii is the reference organism), improves keeping quality, and is verified by the phosphatase test, because the enzyme alkaline phosphatase is destroyed by correct pasteurization.

subjective.question: What is homogenization of milk? Give its advantages.
subjective.answer: Homogenization is the mechanical process in which warm milk is forced under high pressure through very fine nozzles so that the large fat globules (3-10 micrometres) are broken into very small ones (less than about 2 micrometres). Advantages: (1) the small globules do not rise, so no cream layer forms on top; (2) the milk has a uniform, richer taste and whiter appearance; (3) it is easier to digest because the curd formed in the stomach is softer; (4) it is preferred for tea, coffee and processed dairy products. A disadvantage is that homogenized milk cannot be used for cream separation and becomes rancid faster if the enzyme lipase is not inactivated by pasteurization.

subjective.question: Differentiate between casein and whey proteins of milk.
subjective.answer: Casein is the main milk protein (about 80% of total protein). It exists in milk as colloidal micelles with calcium phosphate, is responsible for the white colour of milk, precipitates at pH 4.6 (its isoelectric point) and is coagulated by rennet; it is therefore the basis of cheese and curd. Whey proteins (about 20%) include beta-lactoglobulin and alpha-lactalbumin; they remain dissolved in the whey after casein is removed, do not precipitate at pH 4.6, but are denatured and precipitated by strong heating. Whey proteins have a higher biological value, while casein is richer in calcium-binding capacity.

subjective.question: Describe any three quality tests performed on raw milk at a milk collection centre.
subjective.answer: (1) Organoleptic test: the milk is judged by smell, taste, colour and appearance to reject sour, abnormal or dirty milk. (2) Fat test (Gerber method): a measured sample is treated with sulphuric acid and amyl alcohol in a butyrometer and centrifuged; the fat column gives the fat percentage on which payment is often based. (3) Lactometer test: measures specific gravity to detect added water or skimming. In addition, the methylene blue reduction test (MBRT) shows the microbial quality - good milk keeps the dye coloured for several hours - and the clot-on-boiling test detects developed acidity. Together these tests decide acceptance and price of the milk.

subjective.question: Write a note on cheese.
subjective.answer: Cheese is a concentrated dairy product prepared by coagulating milk with rennet or acid, draining off the liquid whey, and usually salting, pressing and ripening the curd. It contains most of the casein and fat of milk in concentrated form (about 10 litres of milk give 1 kg of hard cheese) and is rich in protein, calcium, phosphorus and fat-soluble vitamins. Cheese is classified by moisture and texture into soft (Brie, Camembert, cottage), semi-hard (Gouda, Edam) and hard (Cheddar, Parmesan) types, and also as ripened or unripened, and processed cheese. The starter culture produces lactic acid, rennet (chymosin) clots the casein, and during ripening, enzymes and microorganisms develop the characteristic flavour, aroma and texture. Cheese is valued as a nutritious, tasty and longer-keeping form of milk.

subjective.question: Describe the main steps in the manufacture of hard (Cheddar-type) cheese.
subjective.answer: (1) Milk selection and standardization: pasteurized milk of good quality is standardized for fat. (2) Addition of starter culture of lactic acid bacteria, which starts acid production. (3) Renneting: rennet (chymosin) is added at about 30-32°C and the milk sets into a firm curd in about 30-45 minutes. (4) Cutting the curd into small cubes to release whey. (5) Cooking/heating the curd (about 38-40°C) with stirring to expel more whey and firm the curd. (6) Draining the whey. (7) Cheddaring: the curd blocks are piled and turned so that acid develops and the texture becomes fibrous. (8) Milling and salting of the curd. (9) Pressing in moulds to give shape and remove remaining whey. (10) Ripening at controlled temperature and humidity for several months, during which flavour and texture develop.

subjective.question: How are cheeses classified? Give examples of each class.
subjective.answer: The most common classification is on the basis of moisture content and texture. (1) Soft cheeses (moisture about 50-70%): high moisture, short keeping quality, eaten fresh or briefly ripened - e.g. cottage cheese, Brie and Camembert. (2) Semi-hard cheeses (moisture about 40-50%): firm but sliceable, ripened for a few months - e.g. Gouda and Edam. (3) Hard cheeses (moisture below about 40%): very firm, ripened for many months, excellent keeping quality - e.g. Cheddar and Parmesan. Cheese may also be classified as unripened (cottage, cream cheese) and ripened (most others), blue-veined (Roquefort), pasta filata or stretched-curd (Mozzarella), whey cheese (Ricotta) and processed cheese made by melting natural cheese with emulsifying salts.

subjective.question: Explain the role of starter culture and rennet in cheese making.
subjective.answer: The starter culture consists of lactic acid bacteria (e.g. Lactococcus and Lactobacillus species). It ferments lactose into lactic acid, which lowers the pH, helps the rennet to act, assists in expelling whey, prevents the growth of many spoilage and pathogenic organisms, and later contributes enzymes for flavour development during ripening. Rennet is the enzyme preparation (chymosin) traditionally obtained from the stomach of young calves. It specifically splits kappa-casein, destroying the stability of the casein micelles, so that in the presence of calcium the milk coagulates into a firm gel (curd) which traps fat and can be cut and drained. Thus the starter mainly develops acid, while rennet performs the actual clotting of milk.

subjective.question: What is whey? Write its composition and uses.
subjective.answer: Whey is the watery liquid that separates from the curd when milk is coagulated in cheese or casein manufacture. It contains about 93% water and about 6-7% solids: lactose (about 4.5-5%), whey proteins (about 0.6-0.8%), minerals and water-soluble vitamins. Although once treated as a waste, whey is now valued: it is used to make whey powder and whey protein concentrates for sports and infant foods, ricotta cheese, lactose for pharmaceutical and food industries, whey drinks, and as animal feed. Proper disposal is also important because untreated whey is a strong pollutant of water bodies due to its high BOD.

subjective.question: What changes take place during the ripening of cheese?
subjective.answer: During ripening (ageing), cheese is stored at a controlled temperature (about 4-15°C) and humidity for weeks to years. Enzymes from rennet, milk itself and the starter and ripening microorganisms break down the curd components: proteins are hydrolysed to peptides and amino acids (proteolysis), fats are partly broken to fatty acids (lipolysis) giving sharp flavours, and residual lactose is converted to lactic acid and other compounds. As a result the hard, rubbery and bland fresh curd becomes softer or crumblier, develops its characteristic flavour, aroma, colour and sometimes eyes (holes, e.g. in Swiss cheese from CO2 produced by Propionibacterium). Longer ripening gives stronger flavour, as in mature Cheddar and Parmesan.

subjective.question: Write a short note on yogurt and its health benefits.
subjective.answer: Yogurt is a fermented milk product obtained by inoculating pasteurized milk with a symbiotic culture of Streptococcus thermophilus and Lactobacillus bulgaricus and incubating at about 42-45°C until it sets (pH about 4.5). The bacteria convert lactose into lactic acid, which gives yogurt its tangy taste, thick texture and improved keeping quality. Health benefits: it is easy to digest, suitable even for many lactose-intolerant people because much lactose is already fermented; it supplies protein, calcium and B-vitamins; and its live cultures improve gut microflora, aid digestion and support immunity. Yogurt is consumed plain or flavoured and is the base for drinks like lassi.

subjective.question: What are the main causes of food spoilage? How can spoilage be controlled?
subjective.answer: Food spoilage is caused by: (1) microorganisms - bacteria, yeasts and moulds growing in the food and producing off-flavours, slime, gas and souring; (2) enzymes naturally present in food, which continue to act after harvest or slaughter (e.g. ripening, browning, rancidity); (3) chemical reactions such as oxidation of fats; and (4) physical damage and insect or rodent attack. Spoilage is controlled by methods that stop or slow these agents: heating (pasteurization, canning), low temperature (refrigeration, freezing), reduction of water activity (drying, salting, sugaring), acidification (pickling, fermentation), airtight and modified-atmosphere packaging, and permitted chemical preservatives, all combined with strict hygiene during handling.

subjective.question: Explain the principles of food preservation by (i) low temperature and (ii) reduction of water activity.
subjective.answer: (i) Low temperature: refrigeration (0-5°C) slows down microbial growth and enzyme activity so food keeps for days; freezing (-18°C or below) stops microbial growth almost completely and greatly slows chemical change, so food keeps for months, though most organisms survive and grow again on thawing. (ii) Reduction of water activity: microorganisms need available (free) water; drying removes water, while adding salt or sugar binds it. When aw falls below about 0.91 most bacteria stop growing, and below 0.60 no microbes grow at all. Examples are dried fruits and milk powder, salted fish and meat, and sugar-rich jams and preserves. Both principles preserve food without necessarily sterilizing it.
